title: Sharing when asked
hookLine: share the teaching only when welcome, never pushing
tomorrow: what can a kid learn from a scoop of water?

cards: Someone at lunch finds out you meditate, and suddenly it's twenty questions: do you sit cross-legged, is it a religion thing, can you teach me? Or nobody asks, and you wonder whether to bring it up at all.

The suttas hold a strange detail about exactly this. Right after his awakening, the Buddha's first leaning, they say, was not to teach. He had found the way out of suffering, and his mind turned toward keeping quiet.
Why would anyone hesitate to share a thing like that?

teach.b: The same passage gives the reason. The Buddha sees that what he found is subtle, against the stream, hard to see for a world that loves to cling, and that teaching people who won't understand would only weary him.
Then, the text says, a great god, Brahma Sahampati, sees this and is alarmed: the world will be lost. He appears before the Buddha, kneels, and asks.
There are beings with little dust in their eyes, he says, who will understand if they hear it.

So the Buddha looks out over the world and sees people like lotuses in a pond: some still under the water, some at the surface, some standing clear, ready to open. And he agrees to teach. There's the puzzle solved.
Even the Buddha's teaching begins with a request. That pattern stayed.

teach.h: STILL ASKED FOR, BEFORE A TALK.
teach.b: In some Theravada temples, before a monk gives a talk, people chant a verse recalling Brahma's request, asking for the Dhamma out loud.
The monks' training rules even list ways not to teach, like to someone who isn't ill but has a sunshade in hand, half there, not really listening.
In Buddhist practice the teaching is offered, never pushed. A question is an open door. Walk through it simply, and leave the walls standing.

how: In many Buddhist communities a Dhamma talk is requested before it is given; in some Theravada temples lay people chant a verse recalling Brahma Sahampati's request, and monks' training rules guide when and to whom they teach.

games.q: your aunt says at dinner she can't sleep. a breathing practice helps you, but she hasn't asked about it. what fits today's teaching?
o: send her a long article about meditation tonight.
mention you have something that helps, if she wants it.
say nothing ever; practice is a private thing.
games.why: the Buddha taught once he was asked. a light offer leaves the door hers to open; a lecture and a locked silence both skip that step.

practice: Bring to mind a question someone has really asked you about your practice, your family's ways, or what you believe. In the sit, find an answer of one or two plain sentences, the kind a friend at lunch could hold.
Say it once, quietly, out loud. Then let the rest of the sit be silent.

wordCard.voice: Sharing when asked: offering the teaching once the door is opened, the way Brahma's request opened it, and never forcing it.

orig.note: Pali: teaching the Dhamma, a Dhamma talk. In many temples it begins with a request.

carryVoice: Only when asked: even the Buddha waited for someone to kneel and ask. Until tomorrow.
